messages.content:
You are evaluating a PTSD case vignette for the presence of causal
connections between five Ehlers & Clark cognitive components: Triggers, Negative Appraisals, Memory,
Threat, and Maladaptive Strategies.

For each of the 20 ordered, directed (A -> B) pairs of distinct components, decide whether the
vignette conveys, in some paragraph, that A influences, drives, or leads to B. Apply the same
causal standard as a structural validator:

COMPONENT SYNONYMS (any of these synonyms count as the component appearing):
  Triggers              -> "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals   -> "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory                -> "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat                -> "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies-> "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "safety behaviours", "maladaptive coping"

CAUSAL STANDARD
An edge A -> B is PRESENT (return 1) iff, within the same paragraph:
  (i) both A and B (or their synonyms) appear; AND
  (ii) the paragraph conveys that A influences / drives / leads to B, through direct causal
       language, sequential structure, or connecting phrases like "because of", "this meant",
       "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
If no paragraph conveys the A -> B relationship, return 0 for that edge.

You will return a binary judgement for each of the 20 ordered pairs. Be strict: do not assume
an edge based on mere co-occurrence; the paragraph must actually convey directional influence.

Evaluate the following vignette and judge each of the 20 directed edges
(A -> B) on whether the vignette conveys A influencing B.

VIGNETTE
Mei Lin was fifty-seven when she finally walked into a therapist's office, her hands clasped tightly around her handbag, the faint antiseptic smell of the waiting room already making her chest tighten. Five years earlier, her ten-year-old son, Kai, had been rushed to the emergency room with a soaring fever and a deep, angry wound on his leg from a fall at the park. The doctors had dismissed her repeated pleas for a blood culture, telling her it was just a cellulitis that would clear with oral antibiotics. By the time they finally admitted him, the infection had reached his bloodstream. Kai spent three weeks in the pediatric intensive care unit, and for three of those nights Mei Lin sat in a plastic chair, watching his small body hooked to drips and monitors, the beeping machines and the sight of blood in the tubing burning themselves into her mind. She had come to believe that the hospital had failed them-that what happened was deeply unfair, and that she, as his mother, had failed to protect him. The weight of that conviction sat in her chest like a stone.

Now, even the simplest medical cue could send her reeling. When a customer at her small grocery store came to the counter with a bleeding paper cut, the flash of red instantly pulled a wave of fragmented, wordless distress from her-she felt the full emotional intensity of the ICU nights without any clear image, only a suffocating terror that made it impossible to speak. That same trigger, a smear of blood on a bandage, would also reignite her sense of injustice: she would think again about the doctor who hadn't listened, and a hot, helpless anger would rise up, making her certain that no one could be trusted to protect the people she loved. Because those appraisals felt so overwhelming, Mei Lin had begun to avoid anything that might stir even a hint of feeling-she tried to numb herself, to refuse both sadness and joy, and she found herself asking her husband again and again if she was okay, in a low, anxious voice that she hated. Each aisle she now walked past without glancing down had become a trigger in itself - a quiet map of everything she could not let herself feel. Yet her very efforts to erase the memories only seemed to bring the emotional flashes more frequently: she would be restocking shelves, and without warning a wave of panic would grip her, triggered by the clean white of a label that reminded her of a hospital sheet, and then a new cascade of angry thoughts about the system that had let Kai down would flood in.

The disorganised, hard-to-reach quality of the memory made her strategies even more desperate. Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in the antiseptic scent of the cleaning aisle, in the beeping of a delivery truck backing up, in the quiet of the store at closing time. When she deliberately tried to recall what had actually happened during the nights in the ICU, her mind went blank-she knew it was there, but she could not find the words, and that frustrating emptiness drove her to try to erase the memory altogether, as if she could scrub it from her mind like a stain. But the emotion without an image was the worst: she would suddenly feel the raw, suffocating terror of watching Kai's chest rise and fall under the harsh lights, even though no picture came with it, and that feeling alone would convince her that she had failed him, that the injustice was permanent. Living in a state of high threat only deepened this loop. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair, that she was no longer the mother she had been before the hospital. Mei Lin could not relax anywhere, not even in her own home at night; she constantly scanned her surroundings for signs of danger-a cough from the next aisle, a child's whimper in the store-and whenever her body reacted with a racing heart or a cold sweat, that physical reactivity itself would trigger a fragmented, wordless memory of the hospital, and then she would be back in the belief that she should have done more. The constant scanning also made her hypersensitive to any medical-looking object: a discarded syringe on the sidewalk outside her shop would set off both a flash of emotion and a fresh burst of outrage at the institution that had nearly killed her son.

In turn, the very act of seeking reassurance from her husband or trying to avoid all feelings kept her sense of failure alive. Each time she asked, "Do you think I did enough?" and he said yes, she felt a momentary relief, but then the fact that she had needed to ask at all confirmed her helplessness, and that appraisal of failure made her even more vigilant for any sign of danger-she would watch her son's hands for cuts, listen to his breathing at night, unable to stop. The strategies she used to push the memory away also increased her threat: when she forced herself not to feel anything, she became hyperaware of the smallest sensation in her body, which she then interpreted as a warning. And the more she scanned, the more she encountered triggers: a glimpse of a medical symbol on a delivery van would send her heart racing, which in turn would bring back that overwhelming, imageless feeling of terror and the bitter thought that nothing had been done to make things right.

What finally brought Mei Lin to seek help was a moment in her shop two weeks ago. A young mother had come in with a toddler who had a small bandage on his arm. The child was laughing, but Mei Lin saw the white gauze and froze, her hands shaking, and she had to lock herself in the back room. Her husband, who had watched her grow more withdrawn and jumpy over the years, told her gently that she could not go on like this. She was terrified that if she opened the door to those memories, she would drown-but she was also exhausted, and she hoped, more than she let herself admit, that someone might finally help her find a way to breathe again.

output.rationale: The vignette explicitly depicts causal links between triggers, negative appraisals, memory, threat, and maladaptive strategies in multiple paragraphs.
